chapter.name: Laws of Motion
chapter.blurb: The chapter asks what governs the motion of bodies and answers with Newton's three laws of motion, starting from Galileo's law of inertia and building up to momentum, impulse and the conservation of momentum. It then treats the equilibrium of a particle and the common forces of mechanics, especially static, kinetic and rolling friction, and applies the laws to a car on a level and on a banked circular road. It ends with the free-body method for solving problems on connected bodies.

scope_in.item: Explain Aristotle's fallacy: a force is not needed to keep a body in uniform motion; it is needed in practice only to counter friction or viscous forces
Describe Galileo's inclined-plane and double-inclined-plane reasoning and state the law of inertia; explain inertia as resistance to change

State Newton's first law in both forms and apply it both ways (zero net force gives zero acceleration; an unaccelerated body has zero net external force), including the book at rest, the car, and the passenger in a starting or stopping bus
Define momentum p = m v as a vector and explain the everyday observations that show force depends on the rate of change of momentum
State Newton's second law, obtain F = dp/dt = m a with k = 1, define the newton, and use the law in one dimension and in components
State the four points about the second law: consistent with the first law, a vector law, applicable to a system with F the total external force, and a local relation
Define impulse as force x time = change in momentum, describe impulsive forces, and find the impulse (as a vector) on a ball hit by a bat or reflected by a wall

State Newton's third law, F_AB = -F_BA, and explain that action and reaction are simultaneous, have no cause-effect relation, act on different bodies, and cancel only as internal forces of a combined system; identify action-reaction pairs
State the law of conservation of momentum for an isolated system, derive it from the second and third laws, and apply it to recoil, disintegration and collisions in one dimension

State the condition for equilibrium of a particle under two, three or n concurrent forces (vector sum zero, triangle and polygon of forces, component equations) and solve equilibrium problems with strings

Describe the common forces in mechanics: gravity, contact forces (normal reaction, friction, buoyant and viscous forces), the spring force F = -k x and tension in a light string, and their electrical origin

Distinguish static friction (self-adjusting, f_s <= mu_s N) from kinetic friction (f_k = mu_k N), state that both are independent of area and that mu_k < mu_s, and solve problems on horizontal and inclined surfaces including tan(theta_max) = mu_s and a_max = mu_s g
Describe rolling friction qualitatively, ways of reducing friction (lubricants, ball bearings, air cushion) and situations where friction is needed
Use the centripetal force m v^2/R and identify what provides it; find the maximum speed of a car on a level circular road, v_max = sqrt(mu_s R g)

Write the force equations for a car on a banked road and use v_max = sqrt(R g (mu_s + tan theta)/(1 - mu_s tan theta)) and the optimum speed v_o = sqrt(R g tan theta); direction of friction for v < v_o and the parking condition tan theta <= mu_s

Follow the steps for solving problems in mechanics: choose a system, draw its free-body diagram, and apply the laws of motion to bodies in contact, bodies joined by a light string on a surface or over a smooth pulley, and a block-and-trolley system with friction
Find the normal force on a body whose support accelerates vertically (yielding floor; a person on a weighing scale in a lift) by applying the second law in the ground frame, N - m g = m a

concepts.name: Aristotle's fallacy, the law of inertia and Newton's first law
concepts.description: Why a force is not needed to keep a body in uniform motion: Galileo's inclined-plane reasoning, inertia, and Newton's first law with its everyday applications.
concepts.idea: Rest and uniform motion in a straight line are equivalent states: both need zero net external force, and a force is needed only to change the state of motion.
concepts.rule: Aristotle held that an external force is required to keep a body in motion. This is wrong: in everyday life an applied force is needed only to counter the opposing force of friction (solids) or viscous forces (fluids), so that the net external force is zero. Galileo argued from motion on inclined planes (bodies accelerate going down, retard going up, so on a frictionless horizontal plane they do neither) and from the double inclined plane (without friction a ball climbs to its initial height, so on a horizontal second plane its motion never ceases). Inertia means resistance to change. Newton's first law: every body continues to be in its state of rest or of uniform motion in a straight line unless compelled by some external force to act otherwise; in simple terms, if the net external force on a body is zero, its acceleration is zero, and acceleration can be non-zero only if there is a net external force. Used both ways: zero net force implies zero acceleration, and an unaccelerated body (at rest or in uniform linear motion) must have zero net external force, the various external forces cancelling out.
concepts.example: A puck sliding at a steady 3 m/s in a straight line on an air table has zero acceleration, so the net external force on it is zero: its weight is balanced by the upward force of the air cushion and nothing is needed to keep it going.

questions.q: State, with reasons, the magnitude of the net force acting on each of these: (a) a drop of rain falling down with a constant speed, (b) a kite skilfully held stationary in the sky, (c) a car moving with a constant velocity of 45 km/h on a rough road. questions.a: Motion on a horizontal plane is the intermediate situation between going down a slope (acceleration) and going up a slope (retardation). So an object moving on a frictionless horizontal plane must have neither acceleration nor retardation, that is, it must move with constant velocity, without any force being needed to keep it moving.

Hence on a frictionless horizontal plane there is neither acceleration nor retardation: constant velocity

questions.q: A passenger is standing in a stationary bus when the driver starts the bus suddenly. Analyse, step by step, why the passenger gets thrown backward relative to the bus and what brings the body back into step with the bus.
questions.a: The passenger's feet are in contact with the floor, and the friction between the feet and the floor makes the feet move forward along with the bus. The body is not strictly rigid: it is deformable, so the rest of the body does not start moving at once but remains where it was because of inertia. Relative to the bus, therefore, the upper body is thrown backward. As soon as this happens, the muscular forces on the rest of the body (by the feet) come into play and pull the rest of the body along with the bus.
s: Friction between the feet and the floor makes the feet move forward with the bus
The rest of the (deformable) body stays where it was due to inertia, so it is thrown backward relative to the bus

questions.q: A book lies at rest on a table. Its weight is W and the normal force on it by the table is R. Student X writes: 'Since W = R, the forces cancel and therefore the book is at rest.' Student Y writes: 'Since the book is observed to be at rest, the net external force on it must be zero, and so R must be equal and opposite to W.' Which line of reasoning is correct, and why?
questions.a: Student Y is correct. The normal force R is a self-adjusting force whose value is not known beforehand; what is known is the state of motion (the book is at rest). The first law then tells us that the net external force is zero, from which we conclude that R equals W in magnitude. Student X assumes the unknown force first and deduces the observation from it, which is the reasoning turned the wrong way round.
s: Judgement: Y's reasoning is the correct one
Reason: the state of motion is what is known; the first law then gives zero net force and hence R = W (R is not known in advance)

questions.q: Design a simple activity, using a small block or ball and surfaces of your choice, that would convince a classmate that a force is NOT needed to keep a body in uniform motion. State what you would do, what you expect to observe and how the conclusion follows.
questions.a: Launch the same body with the same starting speed (for example by releasing it from the same height on a fixed ramp) on to horizontal surfaces of decreasing roughness: a carpet, a wooden table, a polished glass sheet, and finally a surface with an air cushion or wet ice. Measure the distance travelled before it stops. The body travels farther and farther as the friction is reduced, although nothing pushes it in any trial. Extrapolating to the ideal case of zero friction, the body would never stop: it would move with constant velocity with no force acting. So the force we normally apply is needed only to cancel friction, not to maintain motion.
s: Plan: the same body given the same starting speed on horizontal surfaces of decreasing friction
Observation: the distance travelled before stopping grows as friction is reduced, with no push applied
Conclusion by extrapolation: with no friction the motion would never cease, so no force is needed for uniform motion

concepts.name: Momentum and Newton's second law of motion
concepts.description: Momentum p = m v, the second law F = dp/dt = m a, the newton, and the four important points about the law (consistent with the first law, vector law, applies to systems, local in time).
concepts.idea: A net external force changes the momentum of a body, and how fast the momentum changes measures the force.
concepts.rule: Momentum is the product of mass and velocity, p = m v, a vector. Second law: the rate of change of momentum of a body is directly proportional to the applied force and takes place in the direction in which the force acts: F = k dp/dt, and for a body of fixed mass dp/dt = m a, so F = k m a. Choosing k = 1 gives F = dp/dt = m a; 1 newton = 1 kg m/s^2 is the force that gives a mass of 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m/s^2. Points to note: (1) F = 0 implies a = 0, so the law is consistent with the first law; (2) it is a vector law, equivalent to three component equations F_x = m a_x, F_y = m a_y, F_z = m a_z, so a force not parallel to the velocity changes only the component of velocity along the force; (3) for a rigid body or a system of particles F is the total external force and a the acceleration of the system as a whole, internal forces not being included; (4) it is a local relation: the acceleration here and now is determined by the force here and now, not by the history of the motion. The same force acting for the same time causes the same change in momentum for different bodies.
concepts.example: A body of mass 2 kg moving at 3 m/s has momentum 6 kg m/s. A net force of 10 N on it produces an acceleration of 10/2 = 5 m/s^2 in the direction of the force.

questions.q: A truck starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at 3 m/s^2 along a straight level road. At t = 8 s a stone is dropped by a person standing on top of the truck. Neglecting air resistance and taking g = 10 m/s^2, find for the stone at t = 9 s, while it is still in the air, (a) its horizontal and vertical components of velocity, (b) its speed, and (c) its acceleration.
questions.a: (a) At t = 8 s the truck, and so the stone, has horizontal velocity 3 x 8 = 24 m/s. After release no horizontal force acts on the stone, so its horizontal velocity stays 24 m/s. In the 1 s after release gravity gives it a vertical velocity g t = 10 x 1 = 10 m/s downward. (b) Speed = sqrt(24^2 + 10^2) = sqrt(676) = 26 m/s. (c) The only force on the stone is gravity, so its acceleration is 10 m/s^2 vertically downward; it does not keep the 3 m/s^2 of the truck, because the acceleration at an instant is fixed by the force at that instant.
s: Horizontal velocity 24 m/s (unchanged after release); vertical velocity 10 m/s downward
Speed = sqrt(24^2 + 10^2) = 26 m/s
Acceleration = 10 m/s^2 vertically downward only, since gravity is the only force after release

questions.q: A student claims: 'A greater force is always needed to stop a heavier body than a lighter one.' Evaluate this claim using the second law.
questions.a: The claim is not always true. The force needed depends on the rate of change of momentum, that is on the mass, on the speed and on the time in which the body is stopped. A heavier body needs a greater force only if both bodies have the same speed and are stopped in the same time. A light body moving very fast (such as a bullet), or one that has to be stopped in a much shorter time, can need a greater force than a heavy, slow body.
s: Judgement: not always true; it holds only for the same speed and the same stopping time
Reason: force equals rate of change of momentum, which depends on mass, speed and the time taken

questions.q: Design an experiment with laboratory trolleys of different masses, a means of applying a known constant pull and a timer, to find out how the change in momentum produced by a constant force acting for a fixed time depends on the mass of the body. concepts.name: Impulse and impulsive forces
concepts.description: Impulse as force x time duration = change in momentum, impulsive forces, and finding the impulse as a vector when a ball is hit or bounces off a wall.
concepts.idea: When a large force acts for a very short time, the force and the time are hard to know separately, but their product, the change in momentum, is easily found.
concepts.rule: Impulse = force x time duration = change in momentum. It is a vector, in the direction of the change in momentum (and of the force); its unit is N s, the same as kg m/s. A large force acting for a short time to produce a finite change in momentum is called an impulsive force; it is like any other force, except that it is large and acts for a short time, and during its action there is no appreciable change in the position of the body. To find an impulse, write the momentum components before and after and subtract; when a ball is reflected from a wall without change of speed, only the component of momentum normal to the wall reverses, so the impulse is normal to the wall and directed away from it. Average force = impulse / time of contact.
concepts.example: The velocity of a trolley of mass 3 kg moving in a straight line rises from 2 m/s to 6 m/s: the impulse on it is 3 x (6 - 2) = 12 N s in the direction of motion. If this takes 4 s, the average force is 12/4 = 3 N.

concepts.name: Newton's third law of motion and action-reaction pairs
concepts.description: Forces as mutual interactions between two bodies, the third law and the common misconceptions about action and reaction, and identifying action-reaction pairs.
concepts.idea: Force never occurs singly: it is a mutual interaction between two bodies, and the two forces of a pair are equal, opposite, simultaneous and act on different bodies.
concepts.rule: The external force on a body always arises due to some other body. Third law: to every action there is always an equal and opposite reaction; more clearly, forces always occur in pairs, and the force on a body A by B is equal and opposite to the force on the body B by A: F_AB = -F_BA. Action and reaction mean nothing else but force; they act at the same instant, there is no cause-effect relation between them, and either may be called the action. They act on different bodies, so when the motion of one body is considered only one of the two forces is relevant, and it is an error to add them and claim that the net force is zero. If the two bodies are taken together as one system, the pair are internal forces that add up to a null force. The law holds whether or not the bodies are in contact (the stone also pulls the earth). Two forces acting on the same body that happen to be equal and opposite, such as the weight of a body at rest on a table and the normal force on it, never constitute an action-reaction pair.
concepts.example: A book of weight 5 N lies on a table. Pair 1: the earth pulls the book down with 5 N and the book pulls the earth up with 5 N. Pair 2: the book presses the table down with 5 N and the table pushes the book up with 5 N.

concepts.name: Conservation of momentum
concepts.description: The law of conservation of momentum for an isolated system as a consequence of the second and third laws, applied to recoil, explosions and collisions in one dimension.
concepts.idea: In a system with no external force the mutual forces only pass momentum from one body to another, so the total momentum stays the same.
concepts.rule: The total momentum of an isolated system of interacting particles (a system with no external force) is conserved. It follows from the second and third laws: for a bullet fired from a gun, the force on the bullet by the gun is F and on the gun by the bullet is -F, acting for a common time interval, so the changes in momentum are F t and -F t; with both initially at rest, p_gun = -p_bullet and the total momentum of (bullet + gun) stays zero. For a collision of two bodies A and B, F_AB t = p_A' - p_A and F_BA t = p_B' - p_B with F_AB = -F_BA, giving p_A' + p_B' = p_A + p_B. This holds whether the collision is elastic or inelastic; an elastic collision has the additional condition that the total kinetic energy is unchanged. Momenta are vectors and must be added with their signs (directions).
concepts.example: A gun of mass 4 kg fires a bullet of mass 0.02 kg at 300 m/s. Total momentum is zero before and after, so the gun recoils with speed (0.02 x 300)/4 = 1.5 m/s opposite to the bullet.

concepts.name: Equilibrium of a particle and the common forces in mechanics
concepts.description: The condition for equilibrium of a particle under two, three or more concurrent forces, and the common forces of mechanics: gravity, contact forces (normal reaction, friction, buoyancy, viscous force), tension and the spring force.
concepts.idea: A particle is in equilibrium when all the forces on it add up, as vectors, to zero; the forces met in mechanics are gravity, which acts at a distance, and contact forces, tension and spring forces.
concepts.rule: Equilibrium of a particle means that the net external force on it is zero; by the first law the particle is then either at rest or in uniform motion. Two forces: F1 = -F2 (equal and opposite). Three concurrent forces: F1 + F2 + F3 = 0, so the resultant of any two, found by the parallelogram law, is equal and opposite to the third; the three forces can be drawn as the sides of a triangle with the arrows taken in the same sense, and n forces as a closed n-sided polygon. In components: the x-components add to zero, and likewise the y- and z-components. Common forces: the gravitational force acts at a distance without any intervening medium; all the others are contact forces. The component of a contact force normal to the surfaces in contact is the normal reaction and the component parallel to them is friction; a solid immersed in a fluid feels an upward buoyant force equal to the weight of the fluid displaced; viscous force and air resistance are also contact forces. A spring exerts a restoring force F = -k x (k is the force constant, x the displacement from the unstretched state). The restoring force in a string is called tension; one constant tension T is used throughout a string of negligible mass. The contact forces arise fundamentally from electrical forces between the charged constituents of bodies.
concepts.example: Forces of 9 N due east and 12 N due north act on a particle. Their resultant is sqrt(9^2 + 12^2) = 15 N, so the particle is in equilibrium only if a third force of 15 N acts exactly opposite to that resultant.

concepts.name: Friction: static, kinetic and rolling
concepts.description: Static friction as a self-adjusting force up to mu_s N, kinetic friction mu_k N, rolling friction, the angle at which a block on an incline just slides, and the uses and reduction of friction.
concepts.idea: Friction is the component of the contact force parallel to the surfaces; it opposes relative motion, whether impending (static) or actual (kinetic), not motion as such.
concepts.rule: Static friction f_s comes into play only when there is an applied force; it opposes impending motion and equals the applied force, keeping the body at rest, up to a limit: f_s <= mu_s N, with (f_s)max = mu_s N. The limiting value is independent of the area of contact and mu_s depends only on the nature of the surfaces in contact. Once sliding starts the friction falls to the kinetic (sliding) value f_k = mu_k N, which is independent of the area of contact and nearly independent of velocity; mu_k is less than mu_s. For a body pulled by a horizontal force F on a horizontal surface while sliding, a = (F - f_k)/m; at constant velocity F = f_k; with the force removed a = -f_k/m. A block on a plane inclined at theta: m g sin(theta) = f_s and m g cos(theta) = N while at rest; it just begins to slide when tan(theta_max) = mu_s. A box on the floor of an accelerating train is accelerated by static friction, so the largest acceleration without slipping is mu_s g. Rolling friction is much smaller (by 2 or 3 orders of magnitude) than static or sliding friction. The laws of friction are empirical and only approximately true. Friction is reduced by lubricants, ball bearings and air cushions, and is needed for walking, for brakes and for accelerating a car.
concepts.example: A crate of mass 10 kg rests on a level floor with mu_s = 0.6 and mu_k = 0.5 (g = 10 m/s^2). N = 100 N, so static friction can reach 60 N. Pushed horizontally with 30 N the crate stays at rest and the friction is 30 N; once it is sliding the friction is 0.5 x 100 = 50 N.

f_k = mu_k N = 8 N, directed up the plane

(Other acceptable examples: friction on the feet of a person starting to walk, or on the tyres of a car picking up speed.)
s: Judgement: wrong, since friction opposes relative motion between the surfaces, not motion itself
A valid example in which friction accelerates a body (box in an accelerating train, walking, or a car picking up speed)

questions.q: Design an experiment using a rectangular wooden block, a spring balance and a horizontal table top to find the coefficients of static and kinetic friction between the block and the table, and to test whether friction depends on the area of contact. State the procedure, the readings and how the results are obtained.
questions.a: Weigh the block with the spring balance; on a horizontal table the normal force N equals this weight. Hook the balance to the block and pull horizontally, increasing the pull slowly. Note the largest reading reached just before the block starts to slide: this is the maximum static friction, so mu_s = (largest reading)/N. Then pull the block so that it slides at a steady velocity and note the reading: at constant velocity the pull equals the kinetic friction, so mu_k = (steady reading)/N. Repeat with the block resting on a face of different area (the weight, and so N, is unchanged): the readings should be nearly the same, showing that friction is independent of the area of contact. The steady reading is expected to be smaller than the largest reading before sliding.

concepts.name: Circular motion: centripetal force, and a car on a level and on a banked road
concepts.description: The centripetal force m v^2/R and what provides it, the maximum speed of a car on a level circular road, and the optimum and maximum speeds on a banked road.
concepts.idea: A body moving in a circle with uniform speed needs a net force m v^2/R towards the centre, and some real force (tension, gravity, friction, a component of the normal force) must provide it.
concepts.rule: A body of mass m moving in a circle of radius R with uniform speed v has acceleration v^2/R towards the centre, so the force providing it is f_c = m v^2/R, called the centripetal force. It is provided by the tension for a stone whirled on a string, by the gravitational force of the sun for a planet, and by friction for a car on a level road; it is not another kind of force. Level road: forces are the weight m g, the normal reaction N and the friction f; N = m g, and static friction provides the centripetal force: f = m v^2/R <= mu_s N, so v^2 <= mu_s R g and v_max = sqrt(mu_s R g). Banked road at angle theta: vertically N cos(theta) = m g + f sin(theta); horizontally N sin(theta) + f cos(theta) = m v^2/R. Putting f = mu_s N gives v_max = sqrt(R g (mu_s + tan(theta))/(1 - mu_s tan(theta))), greater than on a flat road. With no friction needed, v_o = sqrt(R g tan(theta)), the optimum speed, at which there is little wear and tear of the tyres. For v < v_o the friction acts up the slope, and a car can be parked only if tan(theta) <= mu_s.
concepts.example: A stone of mass 0.5 kg is whirled at 4 m/s in a horizontal circle of radius 2 m: the string must supply 0.5 x 4^2/2 = 4 N towards the centre. On a level road with mu_s = 0.5, a turn of radius 45 m can be taken at up to sqrt(0.5 x 45 x 10) = 15 m/s (g = 10 m/s^2).

s: Vertical: N cos(theta) = m g + mu_s N sin(theta); horizontal: N sin(theta) + mu_s N cos(theta) = m v^2/R

s: Level road: v_max = sqrt(0.2 x 50 x 10) = 10 m/s
Cannot be parked: tan(theta) = 0.45 exceeds mu_s = 0.2

questions.q: A driver claims: 'If I load my car with heavy luggage, the friction on the tyres becomes larger, so I can take a level circular turn at a higher speed without skidding.' Evaluate this claim.
questions.a: The claim is wrong. Loading the car does raise the maximum friction, mu_s N = mu_s m g, but the centripetal force needed, m v^2/R, rises in the same proportion. The mass cancels from m v^2/R <= mu_s m g, leaving v_max = sqrt(mu_s R g), which is independent of the mass of the car. The maximum safe speed is unchanged.
s: Judgement: wrong, the maximum safe speed does not change with the load
Reason: both the limiting friction mu_s m g and the needed force m v^2/R are proportional to m, so m cancels and v_max = sqrt(mu_s R g)

Computes tan(theta) (and the angle) correctly for the chosen values

concepts.name: Solving problems in mechanics: free-body diagrams and connected bodies
concepts.description: The system-and-environment method, free-body diagrams, and applying the laws of motion to bodies in contact, bodies joined by strings over pulleys, and a body on an accelerating support.
concepts.idea: Any part of an assembly can be chosen as the system; the laws of motion apply to it provided every force on it by the rest of the assembly and by other agencies is included, and none of the forces it exerts on others.
concepts.rule: Steps: (i) draw a diagram of the assembly; (ii) choose a convenient part as the system, the rest (plus other agencies of force) being the environment; (iii) draw a free-body diagram showing the system and all the forces on it by the environment, never the forces on the environment by the system (a free-body diagram does not mean that the net force is zero); (iv) mark the forces that are given or certain, such as tension along a string, and treat the rest as unknowns to be found from the laws of motion; (v) repeat for another system if needed, using the third law: if the force on A due to B is F, the force on B due to A is -F. For a combined system the forces between its parts are internal and are not shown. Bodies joined by a light inextensible string passing over a smooth pulley have accelerations of the same magnitude and the same tension acts on both; write F = m a for each body and solve. For a body on a support that accelerates vertically, the normal force differs from the weight: with upward positive, N - m g = m a.
concepts.example: Blocks of 1 kg and 4 kg lie in contact on a smooth table and a horizontal force of 10 N pushes the 1 kg block towards the 4 kg block. System of both: a = 10/5 = 2 m/s^2. System of the 4 kg block alone: the contact force on it is 4 x 2 = 8 N.

questions.a: (a) The block is at rest under its weight 40 N and the normal force R of the floor, so R = 40 N; by the third law the block pushes the floor with 40 N vertically downward. (b) System block + cylinder: weight 20 x 10 = 200 N downward, normal force R' upward. 200 - R' = 20 x 0.5 = 10, so R' = 190 N; by the third law the block pushes the floor with 190 N downward. R' = 190 N (whole system 200 - R' = 20 x 0.5, or the block alone once the cylinder's 152 N push is known)
Cylinder alone: 160 - F = 16 x 0.5, so the force on the cylinder by the block = 152 N upward

Reason: second law for the accelerating block, 30 - T = 3 a with a not zero; T = weight only when a = 0
